Questions / Sourcerer

How do I build software that earns trust?

Powerful tools. Visible reasons. People who can say no.

I want the things I build to be useful without asking people to surrender their judgment. Sourcery explores how software can carry an explicit account of what it does, what permits it, and how a change can be checked.

Follow the questions ↓

A question to practise, not a finished answer.

Sourcerer

The magic has to show its work.

A system can be impressive and still be difficult to question. I want understanding, permission and repair to be part of the design. That means making consequential behaviour inspectable, keeping authority bounded, and distinguishing a promising demonstration from a capability people can rely on.

Where the question becomes concrete.

Permission

Who gave this system the right to act?

A request to help is not permission to do everything. I want the scope of an action to remain clear, especially when an agent or automation is doing the work.

Explore permission →

Understanding

Can someone else see why it did that?

An explanation needs something solid behind it: an explicit description, a source, a reproducible check. Sourcery brings those descriptions and their execution into a common process algebra.

Explore Sourcery →

Change

What would convince me this change is safe to accept?

A successful example is a beginning. I need evidence about the behaviour being changed, its limits and the responsibilities that remain with people.

Explore Temple →

Repair

What happens when my software is wrong?

People need a way to stop, challenge and revise a system. Repair belongs in the ordinary route through the work, rather than depending on the builder being available.

Explore revision →
